strengths: First systematic adaptation of Native Sparse Attention (NSA) to video-language models, with a sensible hybrid design (sparse for video tokens, dense GQA for text tokens) that is well-motivated by the redundancy structure of video.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three task domains (long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, spatial reasoning) against a fairly complete set of token-compression and training-free sparse-attention baselines, generally showing competitive or best results.

Extensive and genuinely informative analysis section (6 findings) covering context-length scaling to 128K, optimal global/local attention budget allocation, branch-wise gating dynamics across layers/heads, latency bottleneck attribution, and — most novel — a detailed study of how the three NSA branches differently induce/avoid attention sinks compared to dense attention.
The finding that sparse-trained QKV weights transfer beneficial inductive biases even under dense-attention inference is a nice additional insight beyond the primary efficiency claim.
Large and detailed appendix with subtask-level breakdowns, hyperparameters, and branch-ablation tables that supports reproducibility of the empirical claims.
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is limited: the method is largely a direct application of the existing NSA mechanism (Yuan et al., 2025b) to video tokens with a modality-split hybrid attention, rather than a new sparse-attention algorithm; the 'attention as GNN message passing' framing in Sec 2.2 is more rhetorical than a rigorous new contribution.

Performance gains over strong training-free sparse baselines (XAttention, MInference) are often marginal or mixed (e.g., TimeScope 83.7 vs 83.1/82.7; VSIBench 36.1 is not the best among sparse methods, XAttention scores 36.6), undercutting the strength of the central claim of consistent superiority.
Only a single backbone/model size (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) is evaluated; no validation at larger scale or with a different base VLM, limiting evidence for generality of the approach.
Project page/code/model links are blank in the submission, and despite a reproducibility statement, key artifacts (trained model, code) are not actually verifiable at review time.

Minor numeric inconsistencies across tables for the same metric (e.g., VideoNSA LongVideoBench score reported as 60.0 in Table 1, 59.4 in Table 3, and 60.2 in Table 7) raise concerns about experimental bookkeeping/consistency.

The fine-tuned dense baseline (Dense-SFT) underperforms the base model on several benchmarks, suggesting the 216K training set itself is of limited quality, which complicates attributing gains specifically to the sparse-attention mechanism versus training data effects.

While latency of branches is analyzed, there is no direct wall-clock/memory comparison of VideoNSA against the token-compression and training-free sparse baselines in the main results table, making the practical efficiency argument less concrete than the accuracy claims.

Many of the 'findings' are descriptive empirical observations without deeper mechanistic explanation or actionable design guidance beyond the specific trained model, somewhat limiting broader significance for the community.

strengths: Adapts Native Sparse Attention (NSA) to the video-language modeling setting, which is a reasonably novel application beyond the original LLM-focused NSA work.

Extensive empirical analysis effort: ablations on branch combinations, information-budget scaling, attention-budget allocation, gating distributions across layers/heads, latency breakdown per branch, and attention-sink characterization.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility information for training (hyperparameters, data filtering criteria, compute budget) and evaluation settings provided in the appendix.

Covers a broad set of benchmarks spanning long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial understanding, together with a decent set of token-compression and training-free sparse-attention baselines.
weaknesses: The core quantitative claim of superiority is weak: in Table 1, VideoNSA's gains over strong training-free sparse-attention baselines (MInference, XAttention, Tri-Shape, FlexPrefill) are frequently marginal or even negative (e.g., VSIBench 36.1 vs XAttention 36.6; LongTimeScope tied with MInference at 44.4; TimeScope 83.7 vs FlexPrefill 83.0), despite VideoNSA requiring 4600 H100-hours of end-to-end fine-tuning while the baselines are training-free. This undermines the central value proposition of the method.

No comparison against other trainable/learnable sparse or efficient-attention video methods; the only trained baseline is the authors' own dense SFT model, which actually underperforms the untrained Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline on several benchmarks, making it unclear whether gains stem from the NSA architecture or incidental training effects.

Several result tables contain unexplained anomalies (e.g., Table 25/29 rows with exactly 0.0 accuracy for certain block/window configurations), suggesting instability or failure cases that are not discussed, raising concerns about robustness and result reliability.

Many reported differences across methods/benchmarks are small enough to plausibly fall within evaluation noise, yet no significance testing, multiple seeds, or variance analysis is reported to substantiate the claimed improvements.

The technical contribution is largely an engineering adaptation of an existing method (NSA) with a straightforward hybrid (dense-text/sparse-video) design; the six 'findings' in Section 4, while numerous, are mostly descriptive/post-hoc observations without strong actionable or theoretical insight, and the writing is dense and somewhat unfocused across a very large appendix of repetitive figures.
Experiments are limited to a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B); no evidence of generalization to other MLLM architectures or model scales.

The project page, code, and model links in the abstract are left blank, raising concerns about the current reproducibility/release status of the artifacts despite the stated reproducibility statement.

Training data is a specifically filtered subset (350–550 frame videos at 4fps) of LLaVA-Video-178K tailored to emphasize temporal redundancy, which may unfairly advantage VideoNSA relative to off-the-shelf baselines evaluated without any task-specific fine-tuning on matched data.

strengths: First work to adapt Native Sparse Attention (NSA) specifically to video-language models with end-to-end training, addressing a real and important problem of long-video context scaling.
Hybrid design that preserves dense GQA for text tokens while applying NSA to vision tokens is a sensible and well-motivated architectural choice.

Extensive empirical analysis across multiple axes: context length scaling (up to 128K), attention budget allocation, branch ablations, gating dynamics across layers, latency breakdown by branch, and a novel analysis of attention sink behavior under learnable sparsity.
Strong efficiency claims are backed by experiments: achieving competitive or superior accuracy using only ~3.6% of the full attention budget at 128K context length.

Broad benchmark coverage spanning long-video understanding (LongVideoBench, MLVU, TimeScope, LongTimeScope), temporal reasoning (Tomato), and spatial reasoning (VSIBench), with appropriate comparisons against both token-compression and training-free sparse-attention baselines.

The attention-sink analysis (Finding 6) is a novel and interesting contribution connecting learnable sparse attention mechanisms to sink phenomena, which could be of independent interest to the broader long-context modeling community.
Reasonably transparent reporting of training recipe, hyperparameters, and evaluation settings in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Performance gains over strong training-free sparse-attention baselines (e.g., MInference, XAttention, FlexPrefill) are often marginal (e.g., VideoNSA 60.0 vs. MInference 59.2 on LongVideoBench; VideoNSA 36.1 vs. XAttention 36.6 on VSIBench, where VideoNSA actually loses), raising questions about whether the added training cost (4600 H100 GPU hours) is justified relative to simpler training-free alternatives.

The method requires full end-to-end fine-tuning of ViT+MLP+LLM, which is a non-trivial cost compared to training-free baselines; the paper does not clearly quantify the trade-off between this training cost and the modest accuracy gains.
Only one base model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and one model scale are evaluated; generalization to other architectures or larger/smaller models is untested, limiting claims of broad applicability.

The training data filtering (350-550 frames, 4fps subset of LLaVA-Video-178K) is relatively narrow and the Dense-SFT baseline shows degraded performance from this data, suggesting data quality/scope issues that could confound comparisons between Dense-SFT, Dense-NSA, and VideoNSA.

Many ablation tables (branch combinations, information scaling, attention scaling) are run on seemingly small evaluation subsets or single configurations without reported variance/multiple seeds, making it hard to assess statistical significance of fine-grained differences (e.g., 0.1-0.5 point gaps).

The attention budget formula and scaling analysis (Finding 3) is somewhat ad hoc; the claimed 'optimal' ratio is determined post-hoc per-task rather than through a principled or generalizable method, limiting practical guidance.

Some odd/unexplained behaviors are noted but not investigated further (e.g., 'strange behavior in the last layer' in Finding 4, inconsistent VSIBench results under budget scaling with some configurations collapsing to 0.0 in Table 29), which undercuts confidence in the robustness of the proposed method and analysis.

The paper is dense with many findings/tables but the core narrative sometimes reads as a loosely connected set of empirical observations rather than a tightly integrated story; some findings (e.g., attention sinks) feel like interesting side explorations rather than central to the main contribution.

No analysis of wall-clock/throughput speedup compared to dense attention baselines in absolute terms (only relative branch latency breakdown is shown), which would be important for substantiating efficiency claims in practice.

strengths: The paper conducts an unusually thorough empirical investigation, including branch-combination ablations, context-length scaling to 128K, attention-budget scaling, gating/inter-head similarity analysis, attention-sink characterization, and efficiency (FLOPs/latency) breakdowns, which together provide useful practical insights for the community even beyond the core method.

VideoNSA is evaluated against a reasonably broad set of baselines (token compression: FastV, VScan, VisionZip; training-free sparse attention: Tri-Shape, MInference, FlexPrefill, XAttention; quantization: AWQ) across three task categories (long-video, temporal reasoning, spatial understanding) plus two additional benchmarks in the appendix (LSDBench, VideoEvalPro), showing generally competitive or best results.

The hybrid design (dense attention for text, NSA for vision) is a sensible, well-motivated architectural choice that preserves instruction-following while enabling scalable sparse attention on the dominant vision token stream.

The attention-sink analysis (Finding 6) and the gating-branch specialization analysis (Finding 3/4) are interesting and provide mechanistic insight into why/how sparse attention behaves differently in video versus text contexts, supported by additional appendix comparisons against text-only NSA.
Reasonably strong reproducibility effort: detailed training hyperparameters, evaluation settings, and dataset construction are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is a fairly direct adaptation of an existing method (NSA, Yuan et al. 2025c) to video by setting block size equal to per-frame token count and applying a hybrid dense/sparse split by modality; the architectural novelty beyond this straightforward adaptation is limited.

Reported gains over strong training-free sparse-attention baselines (XAttention, MInference) are often marginal or mixed (e.g., Table 1: VideoNSA 60.0 vs XAttention 59.1 on LVB, 83.7 vs 83.1 on TimeScope, 36.1 vs 36.6 on VSIBench where VideoNSA is actually slightly worse), making the practical significance of the proposed method less clear despite requiring substantial additional training (4600 H100 hours) that the baselines do not.

Table 3 shows that transferring the learned sparse-trained weights to dense attention (Dense-NSA) sometimes matches or nearly matches full VideoNSA performance, raising questions about how much of the improvement stems from the sparse architecture itself versus the training data/recipe used to fine-tune the backbone.

The efficiency story is weaker in practice than in theory: theoretical FLOPs suggest 0.24x cost relative to dense attention, but the actual implementation only achieves 0.56x FLOPs and modest real-world speedups (per Appendix Q/Figure 26) due to kernel padding constraints from the unusual Qwen2.5-VL GQA head configuration, undermining the "hardware-aware" efficiency claims made in the abstract/intro.
Only a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and single model scale is evaluated; no experiments at larger scale or with alternative backbones are provided to test generality of the approach.

The paper packs in six distinct "findings" plus extensive appendices, which, while thorough, dilutes focus and depth of analysis for any single finding; several analyses (e.g., routing-path stability theory in Appendix M) are somewhat speculative/post-hoc justifications rather than rigorously validated claims.

Comparisons with training-free baselines are not entirely apples-to-apples, since VideoNSA benefits from end-to-end fine-tuning on 216K video QA pairs that the baselines do not receive; the Dense-SFT ablation partially addresses this but a more controlled comparison (e.g., fine-tuning baselines with the same data under their sparse settings) would strengthen the claims.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important problem (scaling video-language models to long context) and is the first to adapt Native Sparse Attention specifically to the video modality via a hybrid dense-text/sparse-video scheme built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B.

The empirical investigation is broad: it covers long-video, temporal-reasoning, and spatial-understanding benchmarks, and includes many ablations (branch combinations, context-length scaling to 128K, attention-budget allocation, gating dynamics, attention-sink analysis, PCA of gate vectors, dense-vs-sparse weight transfer).

Several of the qualitative findings (task-dependent global/local attention allocation, differing branch dominance across layers, distinct attention-sink behavior per branch) are interesting and could be useful observations for the sparse-attention-for-video community.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: training hyperparameters, data filtering procedure, and evaluation settings are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: Performance gains over existing training-free sparse-attention and compression baselines are mostly marginal and inconsistent (e.g., in Table 1, VideoNSA underperforms MInference on VSIBench, and differences on MLVU/TimeScope/LVB are within ~1 point), despite VideoNSA requiring ~4600 H100 GPU hours of full end-to-end fine-tuning (ViT+MLP+LLM) while baselines are training-free — the cost/benefit trade-off is not convincingly justified.

The central efficiency claim (near-linear scaling, hardware-aware sparsity) is undercut by the paper's own appendix analysis: actual FLOPs reduction (0.56x) is far from the theoretical ideal (0.24x) due to query-head padding issues in the NSA kernel, and the measured latency in Figure 26 shows VideoNSA is often slower than other sparse baselines (e.g., XAttention, MInference) at most context lengths, with the compression branch identified as an unresolved computational bottleneck.

The core technical contribution is largely an engineering adaptation of an existing mechanism (NSA, Yuan et al. 2025) to a new modality rather than a novel algorithmic advance; the three-branch hybrid design and GQA-for-text/NSA-for-vision split are relatively straightforward extensions.

Several ablation tables contain unexplained anomalies (e.g., 0.0 accuracy rows in Tables 29/30/33, missing/dash entries, an SFT baseline that underperforms the un-tuned base model on multiple benchmarks), raising reproducibility and stability concerns that are not discussed in the main text.
The theoretical justification in Appendix M (routing-path stability, RoPE phase aliasing) is somewhat hand-wavy and not rigorously connected to the empirical scaling curves it purports to explain.
Writing and presentation quality is inconsistent, with numerous typographical/grammatical errors throughout the main text and appendix, suggesting insufficient proofreading for a top-tier submission.

The comparison setup (official best configurations for compression baselines vs. matched configuration for sparse baselines) is not fully controlled, making some of the baseline comparisons less rigorous than desirable.

strengths: First systematic adaptation of Native Sparse Attention (NSA) to video-language models, with a sensible hybrid design that applies NSA to vision tokens while preserving dense GQA for text tokens, addressing a genuine gap given that most prior sparse attention work targets text or short multimodal contexts.

Extensive empirical evaluation across six benchmarks spanning long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial understanding, with comparisons against both training-free sparse attention baselines and token-compression baselines, showing competitive-to-best results with substantially higher efficiency (3.6% attention budget at 128K context).

Rich set of analyses beyond headline results: context-length scaling, attention-budget scaling, branch ablations, gating dynamics across layers/heads, attention-sink characterization per branch, and comparison to text-only NSA gating behavior — this breadth of mechanistic analysis is unusually thorough for a systems/architecture paper and provides useful insights for the community (e.g., compression branch as latency bottleneck, selection branch suppressing attention sinks).

The appendix provides substantial reproducibility details (hyperparameters, evaluation settings, per-subtask breakdowns) and an honest accounting of practical limitations (e.g., kernel padding overhead causing actual FLOPs to exceed theoretical savings).
Theoretical discussion linking RoPE geometry and routing-path stability to the observed context-length vs. attention-budget scaling asymmetry adds some interpretive depth beyond pure empiricism.
weaknesses: Performance gains over strong training-free sparse-attention baselines (XAttention, MInference, FlexPrefill) are often marginal (sub-1 to low single-point differences) despite VideoNSA requiring expensive end-to-end training (4600 H100 hours) and a fixed 216K-pair dataset, raising questions about whether the cost-benefit tradeoff is clearly favorable versus simpler training-free alternatives.

The baseline comparison is somewhat uneven: sparse-attention baselines are evaluated training-free on top of the untrained Qwen2.5-VL, while VideoNSA benefits from full end-to-end fine-tuning on video instruction data; the paper does not clearly isolate how much of the improvement comes from the sparse attention mechanism itself versus simply additional task-specific fine-tuning (the Dense-SFT ablation helps but doesn't fully resolve this given Dense-SFT underperforms the base model on several benchmarks, which is itself unexplained/concerning).

Some findings are presented with more confidence than the evidence supports — e.g., Finding 1's claim about inductive bias transferring to dense attention rests on a single model/training run without variance/seeds, and several appendix tables show unstable or degenerate results (e.g., Table 29/33 rows with 0.0% accuracy or NSA-SWA entries with missing TimeScope values) that are not discussed or explained in the main text.

The novelty is primarily an application/engineering contribution — directly porting NSA (Yuan et al., 2025c) to video tokens with a straightforward modality-split hybrid design — rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the three-branch NSA formulation, GQA preservation, and gating are largely inherited from existing work with limited new methodological innovation.

The practical efficiency story is weakened by the admission that actual FLOPs (4.68 PF) are ~2.3x higher than the theoretical ideal (2.05 PF) due to kernel/padding constraints, and latency benefits over other sparse baselines in Figure 26 appear modest at mid-range context lengths, somewhat undercutting the 'near-linear scalability' framing in the abstract/conclusion.

Clarity issues: numerous undefined notation inconsistencies (e.g., p^{slc'}_t in Eq. 3 without definition), some figures/tables in the appendix contain unexplained anomalies (zero-accuracy rows, missing entries), and the paper is quite dense with many appendix sections that could have been better synthesized or prioritized in the main text.
